entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Emperor Xian of Han, personal name Liu Xie (劉協), courtesy name Bohe, was the 14th and last emperor of the Eastern Han dynasty of China. He reigned from 28 September 189 until his abdication and subsequent end of the dynasty on 11 December 220.

Born in 142 AD, Emperor Xian ascended to the throne after the death of his father, Emperor Shao, in 189 AD. His reign was marked by a series of military campaigns against the Xiongnu and the Wuhuan, which drained the empire's resources and weakened its economy.

Despite these challenges, Emperor Xian implemented several significant policies, including the establishment of a new capital at Luoyang and the promotion of Buddhism as a state religion. He also oversaw the construction of the Grand Canal, a major engineering project that connected the Yellow River to the East China Sea.

The end of Emperor Xian's reign marked the beginning of the Three Kingdoms period, a time of war and instability that lasted for over a century. His abdication in 220 AD paved the way for the rise of the Wei, Shu, and Wu kingdoms, which would shape the course of Chinese history for centuries to come.

One of the most enduring legacies of Emperor Xian's reign is the impact of his policies on Chinese art and culture. The Eastern Han dynasty was a period of significant cultural and artistic achievement, marked by the development of new forms of poetry, painting, and sculpture.

The historian Sima Qian once wrote, 'The Eastern Han was a time of great prosperity and cultural achievements, but it was also a time of great turmoil and upheaval.' These words capture the complexity and nuance of Emperor Xian's reign, a time of both great progress and great upheaval.

Emperor Xian died in 235 AD, and his legacy continues to be felt in China today.
